meta.title: Video Streaming
meta.summary: Upload, transcode and stream video to a global audience (YouTube style), with adaptive bitrate playback from a CDN.

functional: Creators upload videos up to several GB
Videos are transcoded into multiple resolutions
Viewers stream on any device and network

slos.name: Playback start
slos.sli: Plays that start within the threshold, divided by all plays, measured in the player

slos.name: Segment availability
slos.sli: Segment requests answered successfully, divided by all segment requests, at the CDN

slos.name: Time to ready
slos.sli: Uploads that reach READY within the threshold, measured from the upload-complete event to the status change in the Metadata DB, divided by all uploads

alerts.when: Plays starting later than 2 s burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes
alerts.why: Viewers leave before the first frame. Usually the Playback API, a cold origin or a bad player release.

alerts.when: Player rebuffering ratio above 1% for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Viewers are watching a spinner. Only the player can see this, which is why it is measured on the client and reported by player beacons.

alerts.when: Segment errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 6 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket)
alerts.why: Segments are failing to load, so playback stops.

alerts.when: CDN cache hit ratio below 90% for 30 minutes
alerts.why: Origin storage costs and latency rise as hits fall.

alerts.when: Oldest transcode job above 10 minutes, or uploads ready within 15 min burning the budget 6 times too fast over 6 hours
alerts.why: Creators wait longer to publish, long before anything fails.

alerts.when: Transcoder failure rate above 2% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Some uploads never become playable until retried.

alerts.when: Any message in the transcode dead-letter queue
alerts.why: A chunk failed 3 times, so its video will never become ready on its own. Usually an input format the encoder cannot handle.

alerts.when: View Events consumer lag above 10 minutes for 15 minutes
alerts.why: View counts freeze for creators; the stream absorbs the backlog while the aggregator catches up.

signals.name: Rebuffering ratio and startup time
signals.why: Measured in the player: the only place that sees what viewers actually experience.

signals.name: Origin fetch rate
signals.why: A jump means popular segments are not cached, or the cache keys changed.

signals.name: Age of the oldest job
signals.why: Backlog shows up here before creators complain.

signals.name: Chunks encoded and spot interruptions
signals.why: Interruptions mean redone chunks; a spike explains slow time-to-ready without any failure.

signals.name: Views counted per minute against plays started
signals.why: The business number creators see; a gap against plays started means events are lost or filtered as fraud.

steps: Break rebuffering down by region, ISP and rendition.
Check CDN hit ratio and origin latency for that region.
Check whether the player is stuck on a high rendition: look at the adaptive bitrate decisions.
Check transcoder failures by input format.
Check the dead-letter queue: chunks that failed 3 times keep their video in processing for good.
Check storage events: are uploads triggering jobs at all?

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Two distributions: the site and API (behind the WAF, API responses not cached) and video segments (cached for days, signed playback tokens checked at the edge, an origin shield in front of storage)

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Attached to the site and API distribution: managed rule sets, rate rules on uploads and API calls, bot control. Segment requests do not pass through it

nodes.label: Video Segments
nodes.description: HLS/DASH manifests and 4 s segments per rendition

nodes.label: Transcode Queue
nodes.description: One message per uploaded video, then one per chunk and rendition from the splitter. After 3 failed receives a message moves to a dead-letter queue

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points video.example.com (site and API) at the WAF-protected CDN distribution and cdn.example.com at the segment distribution

nodes.label: Transcoders
nodes.description: Own ffmpeg encoder fleet on spot capacity: one worker splits a video at keyframes, many workers encode its chunks in parallel

nodes.label: Playback API
nodes.description: Video metadata, a signed playback token per viewer and one view event per play. Hot video rows sit in an in-process cache for a few seconds, so the database sees a small share of the ~140,000 plays/s at peak

nodes.label: Metadata DB
nodes.description: videos(id, owner, title, status, manifest_url, views) and chunks_done(video, chunk, rendition); primary-standby across zones

nodes.label: Upload Service
nodes.description: Creates uploads and signs URLs; never touches video bytes

flows.title: Upload and transcode
flows.summary: Bytes go straight to object storage with signed URLs; an event kicks off parallel transcoding.

steps.label: resolve video.example.com
steps.detail: The site and API hostname points at the CDN distribution that has the WAF attached, so creators and viewers reach the nearest edge. Resolvers cache the answer.

steps.label: POST /uploads
steps.detail: A trace id starts here and is copied into every job message, so one upload can be followed from this request through transcoding.
steps.payload:
POST /uploads HTTP/2
Authorization: Bearer <creator token>
traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01

{ "title": "My trip", "size_bytes": 3221225472, "content_type": "video/mp4" }

steps.label: inspect, then forward
steps.detail: Managed rule sets, rate rules (per creator for uploads, per IP for the API) and bot control run at the edge, before the request costs the origin anything.

steps.label: not cached: to origin
steps.detail: POSTs and API paths are never cached; the CDN only carries them to the origin over its warm connections.

steps.label: create multipart upload
steps.detail: The service asks storage for an upload id and signs one URL per 64 MB part. It never proxies the video itself.

steps.label: PUT parts directly
steps.detail: Gigabytes go straight to object storage. A failed part is retried on its own, which makes uploads resumable.

steps.label: upload complete event
steps.detail: Storage emits an event when CompleteMultipartUpload finishes; no polling needed.

steps.label: job v_123
steps.detail: The job message carries the video id and the trace id from the upload request.

steps.label: cut at keyframes into ~4 s chunks
steps.detail: Cutting at keyframes means every chunk decodes on its own and the encoded segments line up across renditions, so the player can switch quality at any segment boundary.

steps.label: PUT 900 chunks
steps.detail: A 1-hour video becomes 900 chunk files next to the original.

steps.label: 5,400 chunk jobs
steps.detail: One message per chunk and rendition (900 × 6). Spread over the whole fleet, a 1-hour video finishes in minutes instead of hours.

steps.label: chunk 17, 1080p
steps.detail: Any free worker takes one. If it crashes or its spot instance is reclaimed, the message becomes visible again and another worker redoes just that chunk.

steps.label: PUT 1080p/seg_0017.ts
steps.detail: Same key on a retry, so a redone chunk overwrites identical output.

steps.label: mark chunk 17 / 1080p done
steps.detail: One row per chunk and rendition, inserted only if absent, so a redone chunk is not counted twice. The worker whose insert completes the set writes the manifests and marks the video ready; if two finish together, both write the same files, which is harmless.

steps.label: UPDATE status=READY
steps.detail: The video becomes watchable; the creator's dashboard shows it as ready on its next status check.

flows.title: Watch a video
flows.summary: A tiny API call for the manifest, then every byte of video comes from the CDN edge.

steps.label: resolve video.example.com
steps.detail: The site and API hostname points at the WAF-protected CDN distribution. Resolvers cache the answer.

steps.label: inspect, then forward
steps.detail: Managed rule sets, rate rules (per creator for uploads, per IP for the API) and bot control run at the edge, before the request costs the origin anything.

steps.label: not cached: to origin
steps.detail: API responses are not cached at the edge: each carries a playback token signed for this viewer, and each records a view.

steps.label: SELECT title, manifest_url
steps.detail: Usually answered from the service's in-process cache; this video was not in it.

steps.label: view started
steps.detail: One event per view, never a database write per view.

steps.label: GET master.m3u8
steps.detail: Video comes from a separate hostname and distribution without the WAF: segments are static, signed files, and a WAF priced per request would cost more on hundreds of billions of segment requests a day than it protects.

steps.label: MISS → origin fetch
steps.detail: First viewer in this region. The request goes through the origin shield, a mid-tier cache, so the misses of hundreds of edges for a newly viral video become one fetch from storage.

steps.label: manifest
steps.detail: Lists every rendition and its bandwidth.

steps.label: HIT, token valid
steps.detail: The edge checks the playback token's signature and expiry, then serves from cache. Popular videos are fully cached at the edge; hit rates above 95% are normal.

steps.label: segment (4 s)
steps.detail: Adaptive bitrate: the player measures throughput and picks the resolution for each next segment, so playback adapts instead of stalling.

steps.label: UPDATE views += N
steps.detail: Counts are aggregated per minute, so the number shown is slightly behind and the database sees a handful of writes instead of millions.

notes.text: Signed URLs keep video bytes off your servers entirely. The service handles a few small API calls per upload.

Popularity follows a long tail: a small fraction of videos gets most views. Edge caches serve those; rarely watched videos come from origin storage through an origin shield, so a video going viral does not send every edge's first miss to storage at once.
Move old, unwatched renditions to colder storage classes; storage is the biggest cost after bandwidth.

Jobs are idempotent per chunk: a crashed worker's message becomes visible again and another worker redoes only that chunk, writing the same keys. A chunk that fails 3 times lands in the dead-letter queue and the video stays in processing until someone looks.
Exact real-time view counts are expensive and not needed. Batch aggregation trades a minute of delay for orders of magnitude fewer writes.

At list prices the estimate calculator puts this design near $1B a month, almost all of it CDN egress for about 0.9 EB a day. Nobody pays list price at this scale: large streamers sign committed CDN contracts at a small fraction of a cent per GB, peer directly with internet providers, and place their own cache servers inside ISP networks (Netflix Open Connect, Google Global Cache), so most bytes never cross a paid link. In an interview, give the list-price number, then say egress is the cost to attack and how.

The WAF fronts the site and API distribution: managed rule sets, upload and API rate rules, and bot control against scrapers and view-count fraud. Segment requests skip it, because a WAF is priced per request and segments are static; they are protected by playback tokens checked at the edge and a private bucket that only the CDN can read (origin access control). Upload URLs are signed per part and expire.

questions.q: How does playback adapt to a viewer whose network speed keeps changing?
questions.a: Transcode every video into several bitrates and split each into short segments with a manifest (HLS or DASH). The player measures throughput and picks the bitrate for each next segment, so quality drops instead of stalling. All of it is static files served by the CDN.

questions.q: A transcoder crashes halfway through a long video. What happens?
questions.a: The chunk's message was never acknowledged, so it reappears on the queue after its visibility timeout and another worker redoes just that chunk from the chunk file in raw storage. Because each chunk and rendition is its own message, a crash costs seconds of work, not the whole video, and long videos finish faster. After 3 failed receives the message goes to a dead-letter queue for a person to look at.

questions.q: Egress is the biggest cost. How do you reduce it?
questions.a: Serve as much as possible from the CDN edge, with long cache lifetimes because segments never change. Push popular content to the edge ahead of time and let the long tail come from origin. Efficient codecs cut bytes per minute, and very large platforms place caches inside ISP networks.

questions.q: How do you count views at this scale without a hot row for popular videos?
questions.a: Never increment a database row per view. The Playback API sends one event per play to a stream; aggregators count them in time windows and write the totals periodically. The displayed count lags by seconds or minutes, which is acceptable, and fraud can be filtered before counting.

questions.q: How do you make uploads of very large files reliable?
questions.a: Use resumable, chunked uploads straight to object storage with signed URLs, so a dropped connection resumes from the last chunk instead of starting over. The upload service only creates the upload and records metadata. When the last chunk lands, an event starts transcoding.

questions.q: The Playback API is read heavily for titles, thumbnails and manifest URLs. How do you scale it?
questions.a: Metadata changes rarely, so cache it: an in-process cache in the Playback API with a few seconds' TTL absorbs popular videos, and read replicas take the rest. The API response itself is not cached at the CDN because it carries a per-viewer playback token and records a view; thumbnails and the page shell are static and are cached there. Invalidate on the few writes, such as a title change or a newly finished transcode.
